passages.happening:
A watchman asks, ‘Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments?’ (verse 1). ‘Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength?’ (verse 1). The answer comes: it is the one proclaiming vindication, mighty to save (verse 1).

‘Why are Your clothes red, and Your garments like one who treads the winepress?’ (verse 2). He answers that he has trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with him. He trampled them in his anger, and their blood stained his clothes (verse 3). The day of vengeance was in his heart, and the year of his redemption had come (verse 4).

He looked, but there was no one to help, and he was appalled that no one stepped in. So his own arm brought salvation, and his own wrath upheld him (verse 5). He trampled the nations in his anger (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The last part of Isaiah speaks to people waiting for the full restoration God had promised. Chapters 60 to 62 painted Zion's glory. Chapter 63 opens with the dark side of that same day. Before Zion can be set right, her enemies must be judged, and the warrior who does it acts alone.

Winemaking happened in a winepress cut into rock. Grapes were heaped into an upper vat and trodden underfoot, and the juice ran into a lower vat. Treaders sang and shouted at harvest, and their legs and clothes were splashed red. The prophets used the picture for judgment, and every hearer would see the splatter at once. There is wordplay too: Edom sounds like adom, red, and Bozrah sounds like the word for a grape harvest.

Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea, traced its line to Esau, Jacob's brother, and had a long, bitter history with Judah. Psalm 137 and Obadiah remember Edom cheering when Jerusalem fell. Bozrah was one of its chief cities. By this time Edom had become a byword for the hostile nations as a whole, as in Isaiah 34.

The key phrases, alone, no one to help, and an arm that brought salvation, repeat almost word for word 59:16-17, where God put on righteousness as armor.
passages.later: Revelation takes up the picture for the returning Christ: ‘He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God’ (Revelation 19:13), and ‘He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty’ (Revelation 19:15).
passages.hard:
How can God be pictured spattered with blood, trampling nations in his anger?

The picture is violent on purpose, and it should not be softened. It is poetry drawn from the harvest, a symbol of decisive judgment and not a battle report. Edom stands for every power that has crushed God's people. The anger is not a mood but justice. The warrior acts because he looked and there was no one to help, so the judgment is the other side of rescue for the oppressed. A God who never opposed cruelty would not be good. And the Bible places such judgment in God's hands alone. It is a reason for the oppressed to hope, not a license for anyone to take vengeance.

Some readers still find the picture troubling, and Christians differ on how final and how literal such judgment is. The New Testament does not retreat from it, since Revelation uses it of Christ. The chapter itself moves from the warrior to a prayer for mercy, as if the right answer to the vision of judgment is to ask God to save.

Edom here is an ancient nation, standing for the hostile powers. These notes identify no people or nation of the present day with Edom, and the passage gives no one a warrant to wish ruin on any people now.
passages.asks: The warrior looked and found no one to help. Ask where you have seen cruelty and assumed someone else would step in. And ask whether the thought of God's judgment makes you afraid, or gives you hope for those who have been crushed.

passages.happening:
The tone changes completely. ‘I will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and His praiseworthy acts’ (verse 7), all the good he has done for the house of Israel in his compassion. God said they were surely his people, sons who would not be disloyal, and so he became their Savior (verse 8).

‘In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them’ (verse 9). ‘In His love and compassion He redeemed them; He lifted them up and carried them all the days of old’ (verse 9).

‘But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit’ (verse 10). So he turned and became their enemy and fought against them.

Then his people remembered the days of Moses. Where is the one who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of his flock, who set his Holy Spirit among them (verse 11)? He divided the waters to make himself an everlasting name (verse 12). He led them through the depths so they did not stumble (verse 13). ‘Like cattle going down to the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
From verse 7 the people pray. This prayer runs to the end of chapter 64, and chapters 65 and 66 are God's answer. After the vision of glory, the community admits how far it is from that vision and asks God to come.

The prayer is a communal lament, a form known from the psalms. It moves from remembering God's past kindness, through confession, to the anguished question, Where is he? It opens with chesed, loyal covenant love, because the people have no claim of their own, only the character of the God who bound himself to them.

The shepherds of the flock are Moses and the leaders with him. The Angel of his Presence recalls the angel who went before Israel in the wilderness, and God's promise to Moses that his Presence would go with them. The word for grieve in verse 10 is used for real pain, including God's grief over human wickedness before the flood. The prayer says the people's rebellion hurt God.
passages.later: God promised Moses, ‘My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest’ (Exodus 33:14), the rest verse 14 remembers. Another lament remembers in the same way: ‘Why have You rejected us forever, O God?’ (Psalm 74:1).
passages.asks: The prayer says that in all their distress, God too was afflicted. Ask what it means to you that God shares the distress of his people. And ask what you remember of God's past kindness that you could bring into a prayer today.

passages.t: Look down from heaven: the LORD as Father
passages.happening:
‘Look down from heaven and see, from Your holy and glorious habitation’ (verse 15). Where are his zeal and might? His yearning and compassion are held back (verse 15).

‘Yet You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us’ (verse 16). ‘You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name’ (verse 16).

‘Why, O LORD, do You make us stray from Your ways and harden our hearts from fearing You?’ (verse 17). They ask him to return for the sake of his servants. For a short while his people held his holy place, ‘but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary’ (verse 18). They have become like people he never ruled, never called by his name (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
These chapters speak to a community for whom Jerusalem's sanctuary had been trampled and the temple burned. Many scholars date them to the decades after the first exiles came back in 538 BC, when the temple lay in ruins or was slowly being rebuilt, finished about 515 BC. Those who hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book read them as prophecy voicing the prayer of a later generation. Either way, the chapter assumes the destruction of 587 or 586 BC.

Calling God Father was rare in Israel's prayers. Here it names the one who made and redeemed a people and is responsible for them. Even if Abraham and Israel, the ancestors, would not recognize them, God is still their Father.

The word redeemer, go'el, was the nearest relative who bought back land or set a relative free. Verse 16 makes it a name.

Verse 17 is bold. It asks why God has let his people stray, as though only he could turn them back. The prayer does not end here. It runs straight on into chapter 64.
passages.later: The next words of the prayer ask God to tear open the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Moses had asked Israel the same thing: ‘Is He not your Father and Creator?’ (Deuteronomy 32:6).
passages.asks: The people call God Father even when they feel unrecognized by everyone else. Ask what it would mean to call God Father when you feel forgotten. And ask whether you can bring God the hardest question, as verse 17 does, without letting go of him.
